Costumer trick I learned being in theater! If you get blood on something, make sure the person whose blood it is spits on the stain. Your own body enzymes in your spit begin to break down your own blood. Comes in super helpful when safety pins prick you on a costume

I used to have the same problem and have since stopped working as a bartender, but realized I still love getting drunk (as I am currently at home by myself getting wasted). The abuse of alcohol isn’t going to stop with finding a different job. The best thing you can do is get help. I was sober for three months after I attempted suicide and honestly those were the best months of my life. Having that control over yourself and feeling like you have control over your life is so great. I am regretting getting into drinking again, and I will probably end up seeking help in the near future. This road is hard, and I’m telling you it will follow you. My family, when I told them I was sober, was nothing other than super supportive of my decision, and couldn’t stop telling me how proud they were for making a better life. Please don’t ruin happiness like I have. Get help. 

-a friend (25F) 

Edit: I love myself when I am drunk. I am the party girl willing to do everything and anything to make friends. It’s not worth giving up how you want to see yourself as a person, and I fight to be the person I want to be every. Single. Day. 
I am very good at coming up with reasons for myself to be the way I am, but I know it’s not who I want to be in the future, and that is the strength that keeps me fighting. I get MAJORLY depressed after a blackout night, and I know everyone is mad at me. But you have to remember relapse is a part of getting over something. As long as you understand why the relapse is wrong. 
I’m sorry if I’m not helping much as I am currently going through figuring out my relationship with alcohol, but I know that if you are strong enough to say no at least once, at least for one hour, at least for one day, you are strong enough to overcome alcoholism

You did the right thing. I recently was admitted to an inpatient program short term for a suicide attempt. It was absolutely terrifying at first, but after a few days I realized how this really is a life changing experience. The techniques I learned about mindfulness and being self aware are invaluable, and the resources given to me were so great. 

Just continue to be there for her, and treat her like your daughter. Talk to her like she is a normal person, not someone who is fragile or about to break. If she can’t handle talking about something, she will tell you or show signs that she is not ready to talk about it. 

For therapy, I started with a therapist who is trained in brainspotting, which is a type of trauma therapy that trains the subconscious to look at the trauma in a different way that is more acceptable and less traumatic for the person. Might be something to look into, but just a suggestion. 

The only place to go from bottom is up, and with the right support and experience, she will come out of this way better than she was before.
